fields.html: Prepare the project set, its quality checks and review gates, and the knowledge wiki.

sections.title: Project set
sections.html:
Every project creates and maintains these LIVE documents: agents, readme, changelog, and glossary.

Two sections of agents guide each change:

  • Conventions: code style, commits, and the command of each quality check.
  • Review gates: the review gates of the project. Without this section, the default gates apply.

Foundation sets up both sections.

sections.title: Quality checks
sections.html:
Implementation runs these deterministic checks, in this order. It repeats them until they all pass. Then the code compiles, has one style, is clean, and has unit tests.

CheckEnsuresExamples
BuildThe code compiles or passes the type check.tsc --noEmit, dotnet build, cargo check
FormatOne code style, with no discussion in the review.Prettier, Biome, dotnet format, ruff format
LintClean code: no known bad patterns, unused code, or risky constructs.ESLint, Biome, Ruff, Clippy
Unit testsEach unit of code works on its own. The change adds tests for its new code.bun test, Vitest, xUnit, pytest

Rules:

  • agents names the command of each check. One command that runs them all is best.
  • Foundation sets up the checks. If a check is missing, the agent proposes a tool for the stack of the project. A person approves it. The examples are not a default.
  • If a project cannot have a check yet, agents says why. The change is not blocked.
  • Each run writes a check-report. The agent reads it, fixes the code, and runs the checks again. This loop is how Implementation corrects itself.
  • The last check-report goes to Verification. The review reads it with the diff.
  • These checks look at the code. Verification looks at the behavior.

sections.title: Review gates
sections.html:
In Verification, an agent reviews the diff against each gate. Each gate gives pass or changes needed, with its findings. One gate with changes needed sends the change back to Implementation.

AIDDbot ships three default gates:

GateThe review checks
SecurityNo secrets in the code. Inputs are validated. Access rules are applied. New dependencies have no known risks.
User experienceThe behavior and the messages match the user stories. The interface is accessible and consistent. Errors tell the user what to do.
MaintainabilityThe diff stays in the scope of the spec. The code is simple and uses the glossary terms. Each requirement has its tests. The docs are updated.

Rules:

  • A project configures its gates in the Review gates section of agents. It can change, remove, or add gates.
  • Without that section, the default gates apply.
  • A gate states what the review checks, not how to fix it.

Independent end-to-end tests

The e2e-test checks the code from outside, so the code cannot shape its own test.

  • Treat every project as a possible monorepo. The e2e-test is its own package. It can use another stack.
  • One agent instance writes the code and the unit-test. Another agent instance writes the e2e-test from the feature files.
  • The e2e agent reads the feature files and the public interfaces of the system. It does not read or change the source code.
  • The code agent does not change the e2e-test. If a test looks wrong, it records a finding.

Change types

The type follows Conventional Commits. It guides the requirements.

TypeUse forRequirements
choreTooling, dependencies, configuration, docs. No behavior change.The check that shows the result works.
refactorInternal structure change. No behavior change.Behavior is unchanged. The existing checks pass.
fixA defect. Behavior returns to what was expected.Always a regression case: it fails before the fix and passes after it. Usually an If … then requirement.
featNew or changed behavior for users.Observable outcomes: typical (When), boundary (While, Where), and error (If … then) cases.

An epic is not a change type. It only groups several specs.

Impact levels

Each change has one impact level. The change type says what the change does. The impact level says how much process it needs.

ImpactWhenFlowSkipsAdds
smallAll are true: one package, one work session, at most 3 requirements, and no change to data, public interfaces, security, or dependencies.A short spec: Goal, one user story, a short Solution, and 1 to 3 requirements. No feature-file and no data model: unit tests check the requirements. The quality checks and the review gates still run. A person approves the spec and the result together, in the pull request.feature-file, e2e-test, test-report—
mediumNot small and not large.The full change flow. A person approves the spec at the end of Design.——
largeAt least one is true: more than one work session, several agents or people on the code, or more than one package. The e2e package and its agent do not count.The medium flow, plus a review-report. The Tasks of the spec track the progress across sessions and agents.—review-report

Rules:

  • In Analysis, a skill proposes the level from the criteria. A skill can check each criterion. A person confirms the level.
  • The impact field of the spec holds the level.
  • Skips and Adds hold document IDs in backticks. Skips lists the document types that the level does not write. Adds lists the document types that the level writes in addition to the medium flow.
  • If a small change grows past its criteria, it stops. It becomes medium: write the missing sections and get the approval before more code.
  • At any level, write a review-report when a requirement fails or the change has findings: lessons about the way of working, what helped, and what got in the way.
  • The change type and the impact level are independent. A fix can be small or large.

Spec

One spec per change. Its title is # <id> - <title>, such as # s0002 - Build the web knowledge explorer. It has three ## sections: Problem, Solution, and Verification. They follow the problem, solution, verification views.

Its META adds two fields:

  • change: the change type: chore, refactor, fix, or feat.
  • impact: the impact level: small, medium, or large.
SectionSubsectionContentWritten inWhen
ProblemGoalWhy the change is needed.AnalysisAlways.
ProblemOut of scopeWhat the change does not do.AnalysisAlways.
ProblemUser stories1 to 3 stories in USERSTORY form: - `US1` - As a <role>, I want <action>, so that <benefit>.AnalysisAlways.
Solution—A technical design that a person who does not program can read: the parts, how they work together, and the decisions.DesignAlways.
SolutionData modelThe entities, their attributes, and their relations, in a Mermaid erDiagram. Use the terms of the domain-model.DesignWhen the change adds or changes data.
SolutionTasksOrdered checklist. Each task has a check.DesignIn a large change, and when tasks help to coordinate the work.
Verification—A checklist of up to 9 requirements, grouped by user story: - [ ] `US1R1` - <requirement>.Analysis; ticked in VerificationAlways.

Rules:

  • Write each requirement in EARS, as the change type asks. The <system> of the pattern is a system.
  • Each requirement belongs to one user story. Each user story has at least one requirement.
  • Codes compose: a requirement is numbered inside its user story (US1R1, US1R2, US2R1). From another document, add the spec ID: s0002-US1R2.
  • Write codes and IDs as inline code. Use a hyphen - between a code and its text.
  • A requirement states only the expected behavior. Its scenarios show how to check it.
  • In a medium or large feat or fix, each user story has one feature-file in the spec folder, such as s0002-US1.feature. The Feature has the user story tag, such as @s0002-US1. Each requirement has at least one scenario, tagged with its full code, such as @s0002-US1R2. The scenarios hold the details of each check: data, steps, and expected results. A chore or a refactor uses other checks.
  • After approval, the spec changes in two ways only: a checkbox is ticked, and the status and updated fields change.
  • An accepted spec can go back to draft only before its implementation starts. Then a person rewrites it and approves it again. After the implementation starts, a problem with the spec goes to the review-report.
  • Failed requirements and findings go to a review-report. The evidence stays in the check outputs: test results, CI runs, or the review of the pull request.
  • If a change needs more than 3 user stories or more than 9 requirements, it is too large. Split it into several specs, grouped by an epic if needed.
  • The scope is the user stories and the Solution. There is no "In scope" subsection.
  • A small spec has only the Goal, one user story, the Solution, and 1 to 3 requirements. Impact levels

Close a change

  1. Check that every task and requirement is ticked. If one is not, the review-report says why.
  2. Set the spec status to done. Do not edit it again.
  3. Update the LIVE documents that the change affects.
  4. Add a changelog entry to its Unreleased section if the change matters to the people who use the project. Release reads it later.

  • An accepted spec can go back to draft only before its implementation starts. Then a person rewrites it and approves it again. After the implementation starts, a problem with the spec goes to the review-report.
  • Failed requirements and findings go to a review-report. The evidence stays in the check outputs: test results, CI runs, or the review of the pull request.
  • If a change needs more than 3 user stories or more than 9 requirements, it is too large. Split it into several specs, grouped by an epic if needed.
  • The scope is the user stories and the Solution. There is no "In scope" subsection.
  • A small spec has only the Goal, one user story, the Solution, and 1 to 3 requirements. Impact levels

sections.title: Quality checks
sections.html:
Implementation runs these deterministic checks, in this order. It repeats them until they all pass. Then the code compiles, has one style, is clean, and has unit tests.

CheckEnsuresExamples
BuildThe code compiles or passes the type check.tsc --noEmit, dotnet build, cargo check
FormatOne code style, with no discussion in the review.Prettier, Biome, dotnet format, ruff format
LintClean code: no known bad patterns, unused code, or risky constructs.ESLint, Biome, Ruff, Clippy
Unit testsEach unit of code works on its own. The change adds tests for its new code.bun test, Vitest, xUnit, pytest

Rules:

  • agents names the command of each check. One command that runs them all is best.
  • Foundation sets up the checks. If a check is missing, the agent proposes a tool for the stack of the project. A person approves it. The examples are not a default.
  • If a project cannot have a check yet, agents says why. The change is not blocked.
  • Each run writes a check-report. The agent reads it, fixes the code, and runs the checks again. This loop is how Implementation corrects itself.
  • The last check-report goes to Verification. The review reads it with the diff.
  • These checks look at the code. Verification looks at the behavior.

docs.title: AIDDbot
docs.html:
AIDDbot

AIDDbot is a framework of reusable skills, document templates, and scripts for AI-assisted software development. It helps teams coordinate work across the software lifecycle, record decisions, and verify changes.

For: teams that build software with an AI coding tool, such as Codex, Claude Code, or Cursor, and students of AI Code Academy courses.

How it works

Every change follows the same flow and has one spec. The change type (chore, refactor, fix, feat) guides its requirements. The impact level (small, medium, large) decides how much process it needs: a small change has a short spec and gets its approval in the pull request; a large change adds a plan and a review report.

  1. Analysis. Write the problem of the spec: the goal, what is out of scope, 1 to 3 user stories, and up to 9 requirements.
  2. Design. Write the solution, its tasks, and a data model when the change touches data. Write one Gherkin feature file for each user story, with the scenarios of its requirements. A person approves the spec and its scenarios before any code.
  3. Implementation. Implement the change, its unit tests, and the docs. Another agent generates the end-to-end tests from the scenarios, in their own package. Repeat the quality checks until they pass: build, format, lint, and unit tests.
  4. Verification. Run the end-to-end tests and keep their test report. An agent reviews the diff against the review gates (by default: security, user experience, maintainability): pass or changes needed. Tick each requirement that passes. Write a review report only if a requirement fails or there are findings.
  5. Close. Freeze the spec. Move durable knowledge into the living documents.

Skills guide the agent in each step. Scripts do the deterministic parts, such as document IDs, metadata checks, and Git chores. See the documentation catalog.

Status

Design stage. There is no usable release yet.

Next step: H1, map the lifecycle skills. See the project plan.

Requirements

  • An AI coding tool that reads AGENTS.md and Agent Skills.
  • The latest stable Bun, when the AIDDbot CLI exists. Skills will run a pinned release of it.

Project documents

  • AIDDbot wiki: intent, glossary, method, and development pages.
  • Project plan: milestones, dogfooding rules, and future ideas.
  • Design system for AIDDbot documents and diagrams.
  • Changelog: notable project changes.
  • Knowledge explorer: a visual guide to the method, project plan, and specs. Run it locally.
  • AIDDbot-legacy: the archived version of the project.

Author and license

Created by Alberto Basalo. Released under the MIT License outside the explorer.

docs.title: AIDDbot Agent Instructions
docs.html:
AIDDbot Agent Instructions

Project status

AIDDbot is in the design stage. The repository holds its wiki, its plan, and its specs. Do not create code, templates, or skills unless the task asks for them.

For project knowledge, start at docs/wiki/index.md. The current milestone is in PLAN.md.

Reference documents

Each topic has one reference document. Read it before you change that topic. Wiki pages follow the page rules.

TopicReference document
Scope, lifecycle phases, building blocks, shared core, inclusion criteriaintent
Milestones, dogfooding rules, findings, future ideasPLAN.md
Change flow, spec, document types, standards, metadatadocumentation catalog
Termsglossary
Wiki model, page rules, sourcesknowledge wiki
CLI command form, script contract, candidate commandsAIDDbot CLI
Bun runtime, CLI development and packagingCLI development
Knowledge explorer, wiki contract of the explorer tablesexplorer development
Folders, skill locations, what shipsscaffolding
Colors, fonts, Mermaid diagramsDESIGN.md
Notable changesCHANGELOG.md

When you change a rule:

  1. Change it in its reference document.
  2. Check the documents that the rule affects, and update them. Include the documents that apply the rule without a link to it.
  3. Record the reason in the decisions table of the reference document, if it has one.

Git and CHANGELOG.md keep the history. Do not add change history sections to the documents.

Way of working

  • Spec-first. Every change starts with one spec: problem, solution, and verification requirements. A person approves it before any code. A small change gets its approval in the pull request. Impact levels After approval, the spec changes only in its checkboxes and its status and updated fields. When the change closes, update the affected living documents.
    • Temporary exception: until the spec template has been used in a change, changes to the wiki pages and the root documents do not need a spec.
  • Change types are chore, refactor, fix, and feat. An epic only groups specs.
  • Impact levels are small, medium, and large. They decide how much process a change needs.
  • Commits follow Conventional Commits. The commit type matches the change type.
  • Conventions for this project are the writing style and script rules below.
  • Skills define the objective, required context, expected outputs, and verification criteria. The model chooses the approach.
  • Scripts do deterministic tasks. Skills do not repeat that logic in prose.
  • Shared core. Do not add CLAUDE.md, .cursor/rules, or other files for one AI coding tool. Shared core

Writing style

Use the terms in the project glossary.

All repository content is in English. Write for people and machines:

  • Short sentences. One idea per sentence. Active voice. Simple words (ASD-STE100 style).
  • Lists and tables instead of long paragraphs.
  • Relative Markdown links. Cite sources for external facts.

Scripts

Follow the AIDDbot CLI and CLI development pages:

  • TypeScript on the latest stable Bun.
  • Before you finish a script change, run bun lint, bunx tsc --noEmit, and bun test. The same checks apply to the knowledge explorer code in packages/explorer/.
  • The explorer reads seven wiki tables. Keep their headings and columns, or update the explorer in the same change. Wiki contract
  • Skills call the exact package version shipped with the skills: bunx --bun --package <package>@<x.y.z> aiddbot <command>.

docs.title: AIDDbot Project Plan
docs.html:
AIDDbot Project Plan

Status: draft. Current milestone: H1.

  • Success criterion. Another person installs a versioned AIDDbot release in their own project. The person completes a real change with the AIDDbot skills and leaves evidence that others can review.
  • Guiding idea. AIDDbot starts from its foundational documents. We order them first, as the AIDDbot knowledge wiki. Then we build the skills, the CLI, and the distribution on top of them, one piece at a time. We test each piece on this repository as soon as it exists.
  • What ships. Other teams get only the skills, the templates, and the CLI. Everything else stays in this repository. What ships

Building order

MilestoneBuildsDepends on
H1 · Base documentationThe AIDDbot wiki, built from the foundational documents, and the map of the lifecycle skills.The current foundational documents.
H2 · Lifecycle skillsSkills and templates that produce the documents of each lifecycle phase and keep the project wiki.H1
H3 · Deterministic CLIThe aiddbot CLI. It takes every deterministic step out of the skills.H2
H4 · Distribution and versionsA versioned release and an installer that installs and updates AIDDbot in a project.H3

Dogfooding rules

We test AIDDbot on AIDDbot. This repository is the first project that uses its skills, templates, and CLI. The outputs are examples for teams and courses.

  1. Start from the wiki. The AIDDbot wiki is the design base. A skill, template, or command applies a rule from a method page. If a rule is missing, add it to its page first.
  2. Use each piece as soon as it exists. The next change in this repository uses the new skill, template, or command.
  3. The tool never blocks the work. If an AIDDbot step is missing or gets in the way, do it by hand and record a finding.
  4. Record every finding. Each change records its process findings in its review report. Findings that change this plan go to the findings table.

How to use this plan

  • Work through the milestones in order.
  • Tick a task when it is done. A milestone is done when its Done when criterion is true.
  • Close every milestone with a findings review. Findings can change, add, or remove tasks. Record each change in this plan.

H1 · Base documentation

The temporary exception in AGENTS.md covers changes to the wiki pages and the root documents. At least one H1 change uses a spec written by hand, to test the spec format.

  • Review each foundational document. List the gaps, overlaps, and contradictions. Fix them in their reference documents.
  • Build the AIDDbot wiki. Move the foundational documents into docs/wiki/ as pages, with index.md. Follow the page rules. AGENTS.md, README.md, CHANGELOG.md, PLAN.md, and DESIGN.md stay at the root.
  • Update AGENTS.md and the links in every document.
  • Check how anchor links work in Obsidian. Decide if the pages keep them or link to whole pages.
  • Define the lifecycle phases, their project loop and change loop, and the structure and business terms of the glossary.
  • Build the web knowledge explorer: a visual site for people that reads the AIDDbot documents. Spec s0002. Explorer development
  • Separate the project loop and the change loop, with the knowledge shelf between them. Spec s0003
  • Apply the naming review: project brain, agents, no impl-plan, feature files in Analysis. Spec s0004
  • Give the explorer maps in layers: an overview, a change loop map with an impact filter, a brain map, and a blocks view. Spec s0005
  • Map the lifecycle skills. For each phase in lifecycle phases and each step of the change flow, state the skills, the documents that each skill produces, and the order in which we build them.
  • Check that the documentation catalog defines every document in the map.
  • Write one change with its spec in docs/specs/s0001-<short-slug>/s0001.spec.md, with META. A person approves it, and the change closes with evidence.
  • Review the findings.

Done when: the AIDDbot wiki holds the foundational knowledge with no contradictions, the skill map exists, and one change has closed with a spec written by hand.

H2 · Lifecycle skills

Build the skills in the order of the skill map. Start with the change flow: Analysis, Design, Implementation, Verification, and Close. Include the Foundation phase and the wiki operations: ingest, answer, and wiki review. Teams use them to keep the wiki of their own projects.

  • Write the template of each document that a skill produces, in templates/. Start with the spec.
  • Write each skill in skills/, in the Agent Skills format.
  • Use each new skill in the next change of this repository.
  • In each skill, mark the deterministic steps. They are the input for H3.
  • Check that no skill or template assumes one stack or language.
  • Remove the temporary exception from AGENTS.md when a change has used the spec template.
  • Review the findings.

Done when: a change in this repository goes through the whole change flow with the skills and templates, and its closed spec is ingested into the AIDDbot wiki with the wiki skill.

H3 · Deterministic CLI

Follow the AIDDbot CLI and CLI development pages.

  • Turn the deterministic steps that H2 marked into CLI commands.
  • Update the skills. They call the commands and do not repeat their logic in prose.
  • Test the commands on fixture projects. The commands do not depend on the project stack.
  • Use the CLI in the next change of this repository.
  • Review the findings.

Done when: the skills of this repository call the CLI for every deterministic step, and the tests pass.

H4 · Distribution and versions

  • Decide the release unit. Recommended: one version for the skills, templates, and CLI together.
  • Decide if the CLI needs Bun on the user's machine or ships as compiled binaries. Teams that do not use JavaScript may not have Bun.
  • Write the installer. It copies the skills and templates to the location of each AI coding tool and pins the CLI version. It does not need a package.json in the target project.
  • Define the release flow: Semantic Versioning, CHANGELOG.md, Git tag, and package publish.
  • Install AIDDbot in this repository with the installer.
  • Prepare a clean repository with its own AGENTS.md. Another person installs AIDDbot and completes a change.
  • Repeat one test with a second AI coding tool and the same shared files.
  • Update the README.md with the tested steps. Add notable changes to CHANGELOG.md.
  • Review the findings.

Done when: the success criterion is true. The README states how to install, update, and load AIDDbot in each tool.

Findings

#FindingStatus
F1The repository had only 2 of the 5 documents of the old project set.Closed. The project set is now AGENTS.md, README.md, CHANGELOG.md, and GLOSSARY.md. The repository has all four.
F2AGENTS.md already contains the conventions. A separate conventions document is redundant in small projects.Closed. Conventions are a section of AGENTS.md.
F3The catalog did not fix the folders for source documents.Closed. The scaffolding page states each folder and the milestone that creates it.
F4Without templates, the spec-first rule blocks changes to the foundational documents.Open. Temporary exception in AGENTS.md. H2 removes it.
F5The old plan built a template, skill, or script only after we repeated a task three times. It ignored the design in the foundational documents and delayed the lifecycle skills.Closed. The plan now starts from the foundational documents and builds in four milestones.
F6The test install of the CLI used bun add -d. Many projects have no package.json.Open. H4 defines an install that does not depend on the project stack.
F7The old plan deferred the wiki. AIDDbot needs one for its own documents, and teams need one for their projects.Closed. H1 builds the AIDDbot wiki. H2 adds the wiki skills.

Future ideas

Names only. Design one when a real change needs it.

  • Regulated profile (brd, srs, use-case, traceability) and prd.
  • Optional integrations for each tool, such as hooks.
  • Monitoring log and performance budget.
  • Customization for each project (.aiddbot/).
  • Wiki log and automatic ingest on change close.
  • Ontology, if a real consumer needs it.
  • Catalog documents and standards that are not used today.

docs.title: AIDDbot Design System
docs.html:
AIDDbot Design System

Overview

Use this visual identity for AIDDbot visual outputs: documents and diagrams. Use dark surfaces and clear labels. Blue marks what the reader can act on. Green marks what is important. Testing Inteligente stylesheet

Brand mark

Use the original icon beside the text AIDDbot. Keep its proportions and colors. Original PNG

Open question: AIDDbot uses the author's icon for now. Decide later if AIDDbot needs its own logo.

Colors

The tokens without a prefix are the default dark theme. The light- tokens are the light theme. Each light- token replaces the token with the same name. The brand accents apply in both themes. Use the light theme for documents and print.

  • Use canvas for the page and surface for cards, tables, and code blocks. Pair both with on-surface for main text and muted for secondary text.
  • Draw a 1px outline border around cards and tables. surface alone is too close to canvas.
  • Blue means "you can act on it". Use primary for every element that the reader can act on: links, buttons, controls, boxes that are links, hover, and keyboard focus. Pair solid blue buttons with on-primary text.
  • Green means "you cannot act on it, but it is important". Use accent only for elements that the reader cannot act on: borders of important boxes, the current page, highlighted connections, highlighted text, and decoration. Pair solid green fills with on-accent text.
  • Never use accent on an element that the reader can act on.
  • Do not use accent as a status. A status always has its text label.
  • Use the status colors with a text label, never alone:
    • verified green for checks that pass.
    • warning amber for conflicts, open questions, and risks.
    • danger red for failed checks and errors.
  • Use brand-blue and brand-green only for the brand mark and for illustrations. In a user interface, use primary and accent. brand-green does not have enough contrast for text on the light theme.
  • Verify 4.5:1 contrast for regular text and 3:1 for required visual cues. WCAG 2.2

Typography

  • Use display (Audiowide) for the wordmark and titles.
  • Use Roboto for reading text, controls, tables, and section headings: headline-md, headline-sm, body-md, and label-sm.
  • Use code (Fira Code) for commands, source code, paths, and document IDs. Its ligatures are off, so the reader sees each character.
  • Fallback fonts: system-ui, sans-serif after Audiowide and Roboto; ui-monospace, Consolas, monospace after Fira Code.
  • All three fonts use the SIL Open Font License. Host them with the artifact or embed them in exported files.

Mermaid diagrams

In repository Markdown, use only the portable subset. It renders in GitHub, VS Code, and older Mermaid versions:

  • Diagram types: graph (with LR or TD) and sequenceDiagram.
  • Node IDs: letters and digits only, such as ChangeType. Put the visible text in square brackets: ChangeType[Change type].
  • Edges: --> for a relationship and -.-> for a secondary one, such as "is a". Put the label between bars: A -->|has| B.
  • Do not use styles, classes, themes, init directives, icons, HTML, or new diagram types. Put counts and other details in a table next to the diagram.
  • Do not set a theme. GitHub adapts the diagram to the reader's theme.
  • Label nodes and connections. Give each diagram a text equivalent.

Changelog

This file tracks notable changes to AIDDbot. It follows Keep a Changelog and uses Semantic Versioning.

Unreleased

Changed

  • Maintainers publish the explorer on demand with bun run explorer:publish. The command builds the site locally from origin/main and pushes it to GitHub Pages.
  • The explorer gives the information in layers (s0005). The overview at #/ shows the phases, the project brain as one box, and the steps. The change loop map (#/map/change) shows the document types of each step, with a filter of impact level. The brain map (#/map/brain) shows who writes and reads each brain document. The explorer applies the rule: boxes that are links have a blue border.

Each name is used once. The lifecycle phases table has the columns Work, Uses, and Produces, like the change flow. (s0003)

Each file name starts with the spec ID, so an editor tab shows which change it is. Specs s0001 and s0002 moved to their folders.

docs.title: AIDDbot CLI
docs.html:
AIDDbot CLI

Scripts do the deterministic tasks of AIDDbot, such as document IDs, metadata checks, and Git chores. Skills call them. See building blocks.

Status: draft. There is no CLI yet.

Command form

All scripts ship in one executable, aiddbot. Each task is a subcommand: aiddbot <group> <action> [args].

Prerequisite

Bun must be installed on the user's machine. The README states this. If Bun is missing, the skill shows a clear message and an install link. It never fails silently.

This prerequisite is under review. Teams that do not use JavaScript may not have Bun. Compiled binaries can remove it.

Execution from skills

Skills call a pinned version:

bunx --bun --package <package>@<x.y.z> aiddbot <command> [args]
  • --bun runs the entry point with Bun. It goes before the executable name.
  • <x.y.z> is the exact version that ships with the skills. Updates are deliberate.
  • A pinned version comes from Bun's global cache. There is no registry request on each call. bunx reference
  • Do not use @latest. It asks the registry on every run, which is slow, and it runs new versions without review, which is a supply-chain risk.

Script contract

Every subcommand follows these rules:

AspectRule
InputArguments and flags only. No interactive prompts.

docs.html:
AIDDbot CLI Development

How we build the AIDDbot CLI. Its command form, prerequisite, and contract are in that page.

Status: draft. There is no CLI yet. It comes in H3, from the deterministic steps that the skills mark in H2.

Runtime and development

  • Runtime: latest stable Bun. It is the only runtime and toolchain. Upgrade guide
  • Language: TypeScript. Bun runs the source files directly. Bun TypeScript
  • Tests: TypeScript with bun:test. Bun test runner
TaskCommand
Run a script from the repository rootbun run ./packages/cli/src/cli.ts <command> [args]
Lintbun lint (Bun linter)
Type-checkbunx tsc --noEmit (Bun strips types without checking them)
Testbun test

Run the lint, type check, and tests before you close a change to scripts.

Packaging

The package lives at packages/cli/. Scaffolding

  • One npm package with one executable, aiddbot, declared in the bin field.
  • The entry point loads each subcommand lazily (await import(...)). A call loads only the code of its subcommand.

Reasons: one help screen, one version to pin, one bin.

H4 decides if the CLI also ships as compiled binaries.

Before the first publish

Until the package is on npm, test a skill that needs the CLI with a local package file:

  1. In this repository, run bun pm pack in packages/cli/. It creates <package>-<x.y.z>.tgz. bun pm pack
  2. Install that file in the test repository without a change to the project manifest. Many projects have no package.json. H4 defines the exact steps (finding F6).
  3. Record the file name and the repository revision in the evidence of the test.

When the package is published, change the skill call to the pinned form.

docs.title: AIDDbot Documentation Catalog
docs.html:
AIDDbot Documentation Catalog

The documents that AIDDbot uses, the rules for each change, and the standards that the templates follow. See the intent.

Status: draft. The catalog defines the documents that the lifecycle skills produce. The others are names for later.

Principles

  1. Spec-first, not spec-anchored. Every change starts with a spec. A person approves its problem, solution, and requirements before any code. A small change gets this approval in its pull request. Impact levels The spec drives the change and is frozen when the change closes. It is not maintained afterwards. After approval, only its checkboxes and its status and updated fields change. Böckeler on SDD levels
  2. One spec per change. Separate documents appear only when the impact level asks for them.
  3. Living knowledge is harvested, not anchored. When a change closes, durable knowledge moves to the living documents that it affects: glossary, ADRs, wiki pages, changelog.
  4. Fewer documents, more sections. If content always travels with another document, it is a section of that document.

Tags

Each document has three tags.

Life

CodeLifeRule
LIVELivingMaintained for the whole project. Updated when knowledge changes.
CHGChangeWritten for one change. Frozen with status done when the change closes. A later change writes a new document.

Relevance

CodeRelevanceRule
MUSTRequiredAlways produce it. A skill blocks completion without it.
SHOULDRecommendedProduce it by default. Skip it only with a written reason.
COULDOptionalProduce it only when its condition is true.

Form

CodeFormRule
DOCDocumentText for people and agents. The LIVE documents with this form are the project brain.
CODECodeSource code and tests that tools run.

The knowledge explorer reads this table. Keep its anchor and its columns.

Project set

Every project creates and maintains these LIVE documents: agents, readme, changelog, and glossary.

Two sections of agents guide each change:

  • Conventions: code style, commits, and the command of each quality check.
  • Review gates: the review gates of the project. Without this section, the default gates apply.

Foundation sets up both sections.

Change flow

The change flow is the work of the Development lifecycle phase. Every change follows five steps. A step is change level. Its name is not the name of a phase.

#StepWorkUsesProduces
1AnalysisWrite the Problem section and the requirements of the spec. Write one feature-file for each user story, with declarative scenarios of its requirements and no interface steps. Clarify the open questions with a person. Update the roadmap when the work splits into several changes.roadmap, glossary, wiki-page, domain-model, adr, agentsspec, feature-file, roadmap
2DesignWrite the Solution section and its tasks. Add a data model when the change touches data. Write an adr for a significant, hard-to-reverse decision. A person approves the whole spec and its scenarios.spec, feature-file, wiki-page, domain-model, design-systemspec, adr
3ImplementationImplement the change, its unit tests, and the docs. Another agent instance generates the e2e-test from the feature files, with the same tags. It works only in the e2e package and does not read or change the source code. Run the quality checks: build, format, lint, and unit tests. Read the check-report, fix the code, and repeat until they all pass.spec, feature-file, agentscode, unit-test, e2e-test, check-report, and docs
4VerificationRun the e2e-test. It writes a test-report with the result of each requirement. An agent reviews the diff against the review gates and decides: pass or changes needed. Tick each requirement that passes. If a requirement fails or the change has findings, write a review-report. Impact levelsspec, e2e-test, code, check-report, agentsspec, test-report, review-report
5CloseFreeze the spec and harvest the knowledge. Close a changespec, review-reportglossary, domain-model, wiki-page, changelog
  • Uses and Produces hold document IDs from the document catalog, in backticks. Other text is plain.
  • The knowledge explorer reads this table. Keep its anchor and its columns. Page rules

Close is the last step of a change, not a lifecycle phase. Many changes close before one Release. Analysis and Design can happen in one session, before the approval. A small change follows a shorter flow. Impact levels

When the agent review asks for changes, the change goes back to Implementation.

Quality checks

Implementation runs these deterministic checks, in this order. It repeats them until they all pass. Then the code compiles, has one style, is clean, and has unit tests.

CheckEnsuresExamples
BuildThe code compiles or passes the type check.tsc --noEmit, dotnet build, cargo check
FormatOne code style, with no discussion in the review.Prettier, Biome, dotnet format, ruff format
LintClean code: no known bad patterns, unused code, or risky constructs.ESLint, Biome, Ruff, Clippy
Unit testsEach unit of code works on its own. The change adds tests for its new code.bun test, Vitest, xUnit, pytest

Rules:

  • agents names the command of each check. One command that runs them all is best.
  • Foundation sets up the checks. If a check is missing, the agent proposes a tool for the stack of the project. A person approves it. The examples are not a default.
  • If a project cannot have a check yet, agents says why. The change is not blocked.
  • Each run writes a check-report. The agent reads it, fixes the code, and runs the checks again. This loop is how Implementation corrects itself.
  • The last check-report goes to Verification. The review reads it with the diff.
  • These checks look at the code. Verification looks at the behavior.

Independent end-to-end tests

The e2e-test checks the code from outside, so the code cannot shape its own test.

  • Treat every project as a possible monorepo. The e2e-test is its own package. It can use another stack.
  • One agent instance writes the code and the unit-test. Another agent instance writes the e2e-test from the feature files.
  • The e2e agent reads the feature files and the public interfaces of the system. It does not read or change the source code.
  • The code agent does not change the e2e-test. If a test looks wrong, it records a finding.

Review gates

In Verification, an agent reviews the diff against each gate. Each gate gives pass or changes needed, with its findings. One gate with changes needed sends the change back to Implementation.

AIDDbot ships three default gates:

GateThe review checks
SecurityNo secrets in the code. Inputs are validated. Access rules are applied. New dependencies have no known risks.
User experienceThe behavior and the messages match the user stories. The interface is accessible and consistent. Errors tell the user what to do.
MaintainabilityThe diff stays in the scope of the spec. The code is simple and uses the glossary terms. Each requirement has its tests. The docs are updated.

Rules:

  • A project configures its gates in the Review gates section of agents. It can change, remove, or add gates.
  • Without that section, the default gates apply.
  • A gate states what the review checks, not how to fix it.

Change types

The type follows Conventional Commits. It guides the requirements.

TypeUse forRequirements
choreTooling, dependencies, configuration, docs. No behavior change.The check that shows the result works.
refactorInternal structure change. No behavior change.Behavior is unchanged. The existing checks pass.
fixA defect. Behavior returns to what was expected.Always a regression case: it fails before the fix and passes after it. Usually an If … then requirement.
featNew or changed behavior for users.Observable outcomes: typical (When), boundary (While, Where), and error (If … then) cases.

An epic is not a change type. It only groups several specs.

Impact levels

Each change has one impact level. The change type says what the change does. The impact level says how much process it needs.

ImpactWhenFlowSkipsAdds
smallAll are true: one package, one work session, at most 3 requirements, and no change to data, public interfaces, security, or dependencies.A short spec: Goal, one user story, a short Solution, and 1 to 3 requirements. No feature-file and no data model: unit tests check the requirements. The quality checks and the review gates still run. A person approves the spec and the result together, in the pull request.feature-file, e2e-test, test-report—
mediumNot small and not large.The full change flow. A person approves the spec at the end of Design.——
largeAt least one is true: more than one work session, several agents or people on the code, or more than one package. The e2e package and its agent do not count.The medium flow, plus a review-report. The Tasks of the spec track the progress across sessions and agents.—review-report

Rules:

  • In Analysis, a skill proposes the level from the criteria. A skill can check each criterion. A person confirms the level.
  • The impact field of the spec holds the level.
  • Skips and Adds hold document IDs in backticks. Skips lists the document types that the level does not write. Adds lists the document types that the level writes in addition to the medium flow.
  • If a small change grows past its criteria, it stops. It becomes medium: write the missing sections and get the approval before more code.
  • At any level, write a review-report when a requirement fails or the change has findings: lessons about the way of working, what helped, and what got in the way.
  • The change type and the impact level are independent. A fix can be small or large.

Spec

One spec per change. Its title is # <id> - <title>, such as # s0002 - Build the web knowledge explorer. It has three ## sections: Problem, Solution, and Verification. They follow the problem, solution, verification views.

Its META adds two fields:

  • change: the change type: chore, refactor, fix, or feat.
  • impact: the impact level: small, medium, or large.
SectionSubsectionContentWritten inWhen
ProblemGoalWhy the change is needed.AnalysisAlways.
ProblemOut of scopeWhat the change does not do.AnalysisAlways.
ProblemUser stories1 to 3 stories in USERSTORY form: - `US1` - As a <role>, I want <action>, so that <benefit>.AnalysisAlways.
Solution—A technical design that a person who does not program can read: the parts, how they work together, and the decisions.DesignAlways.
SolutionData modelThe entities, their attributes, and their relations, in a Mermaid erDiagram. Use the terms of the domain-model.DesignWhen the change adds or changes data.
SolutionTasksOrdered checklist. Each task has a check.DesignIn a large change, and when tasks help to coordinate the work.
Verification—A checklist of up to 9 requirements, grouped by user story: - [ ] `US1R1` - <requirement>.Analysis; ticked in VerificationAlways.

Rules:

  • Write each requirement in EARS, as the change type asks. The <system> of the pattern is a system.
  • Each requirement belongs to one user story. Each user story has at least one requirement.
  • Codes compose: a requirement is numbered inside its user story (US1R1, US1R2, US2R1). From another document, add the spec ID: s0002-US1R2.
  • Write codes and IDs as inline code. Use a hyphen - between a code and its text.
  • A requirement states only the expected behavior. Its scenarios show how to check it.
  • In a medium or large feat or fix, each user story has one feature-file in the spec folder, such as s0002-US1.feature. The Feature has the user story tag, such as @s0002-US1. Each requirement has at least one scenario, tagged with its full code, such as @s0002-US1R2. The scenarios hold the details of each check: data, steps, and expected results. A chore or a refactor uses other checks.
  • After approval, the spec changes in two ways only: a checkbox is ticked, and the status and updated fields change.
  • An accepted spec can go back to draft only before its implementation starts. Then a person rewrites it and approves it again. After the implementation starts, a problem with the spec goes to the review-report.
  • Failed requirements and findings go to a review-report. The evidence stays in the check outputs: test results, CI runs, or the review of the pull request.
  • If a change needs more than 3 user stories or more than 9 requirements, it is too large. Split it into several specs, grouped by an epic if needed.
  • The scope is the user stories and the Solution. There is no "In scope" subsection.
  • A small spec has only the Goal, one user story, the Solution, and 1 to 3 requirements. Impact levels

Close a change

  1. Check that every task and requirement is ticked. If one is not, the review-report says why.
  2. Set the spec status to done. Do not edit it again.
  3. Update the LIVE documents that the change affects.
  4. Add a changelog entry to its Unreleased section if the change matters to the people who use the project. Release reads it later.

Document catalog

IDDocumentLifeFormRelevanceStandardsPurpose
readmeREADMELIVEDOCMUST—Understand the project, set it up, and make a first change.
glossaryGlossaryLIVEDOCMUSTMETAShared terms for people, agents, documents, and code.
wiki-pageKnowledge wiki pageLIVEDOCSHOULDLLMWIKI, METAOne topic, linked to its sources. See the knowledge wiki.

Metadata (META)

Every Markdown document starts with YAML frontmatter, except the three documents named below:

---
id: s0001               # Unique document ID
type: spec              # document ID from this catalog
change: feat            # spec only: chore | refactor | fix | feat
impact: medium          # spec only: small | medium | large
title: Add the spec template
status: draft           # draft | proposed | accepted | done | superseded | deprecated
created: 2026-11-24     # ISO 8601 date of creation; never changes
updated: 2026-11-24     # ISO 8601 date of the last content change
links:
  sources: []           # evidence and inputs
  related: []           # other document IDs
  supersedes: []        # document IDs this one replaces
---

Use dates without time. Git keeps the history of status changes.

In DESIGN.md, put the META fields under aiddbot in the same YAML frontmatter. Keep the design format keys at the top level.

agents, readme, and changelog have no META. Tools and people read them at fixed names, and frontmatter shows as noise there. Files that are not Markdown have no META: feature-file, code, unit-test, e2e-test, check-report, and test-report.

Document IDs and file names

DocumentidFile
specs<NNNN>: one sequence with four digits for all change types, such as s0001.docs/specs/s<NNNN>-<short-slug>/s<NNNN>.spec.md
review-reportThe spec ID with a suffix: s0001-review.docs/specs/s<NNNN>-<short-slug>/s<NNNN>.review.md
Wiki pageThe file name without .md.docs/wiki/<topic>.md
roadmaproadmap. One per project.PLAN.md
design-systemdesign-system. One per project.DESIGN.md
domain-modeldomain-model. One per project.docs/wiki/domain-model.md
feature-fileNo id. Its Feature tag names it, such as @s0001-US1.docs/specs/s<NNNN>-<short-slug>/s<NNNN>-US<n>.feature
code, unit-testNo id.The folders of the project. agents names them.
e2e-testNo id.Its own package, such as packages/e2e/. It can use another stack. agents names it.
check-report, test-reportNo id.The output of the check command or the test command. Git does not keep it. CI keeps the report of each pull request.
  • Each change has one folder, docs/specs/s<NNNN>-<short-slug>/. All its change documents go in it.
  • <short-slug> uses lowercase words joined by hyphens.
  • The ID does not show the change type. The change field holds it, so a spec can change its type without a new file name.
  • The adr IDs and file names are decided with the first ADR.
  • The rule is provisional. The spec template in H2 confirms or changes it (decision 11).

Status use

StatusMeaningSet inUsed by
draftThe document is in progress. It can change.Foundation, Analysisspec, review-report, glossary, wiki-page, roadmap, design-system, domain-model
proposedA decision waits for human approval.Designadr
acceptedA person approved it. A LIVE document is then updated in place.Designspec, review-report, adr, glossary, wiki-page, roadmap, design-system, domain-model

supersededA newer document replaces it.Designadr
deprecatedIt no longer applies, and nothing replaces it.Designadr
  • The statuses of one document type follow the table order. An adr ends as superseded or deprecated.
  • Used by holds document IDs. The life tag is not enough, because an adr is LIVE with its own cycle.
  • The knowledge explorer reads this table. Keep its anchor and its columns.

Standards

Documents without a standard use plain Markdown and META. Add a standard only when a real change needs it.

CodeStandardPattern or contentUsed by
CONVCOMMITConventional Commits<type>(<scope>): <description>Change types, commits, changelog
USERSTORYUser storyAs a <role>, I want <action>, so that <benefit>.spec user stories
EARSEasy Approach to Requirements SyntaxThe <system> shall <response>, with an optional When <trigger>, While <state>, Where <feature>, or If <condition>, thenspec requirements
GHERKINGherkinFeature, Scenario, Given, When, Then, and @tagsfeature-file
DDDDomain-Driven DesignUbiquitous language, bounded contexts, aggregates, entities, value objectsdomain-model
MERMAIDMermaid ER diagramerDiagram with entities, attributes, and relationsspec data model, domain-model
MADRMADRContext, drivers, options, outcome, consequencesadr

Other documents and standards

Names only. Add one to the tables above when a lifecycle skill needs it.

  • Documents: conventions (a section of agents for now), impl-plan (the Tasks of the spec for now), prd, decision-note, vision, business-rules, process-model, example-map, quality-attrs, tech-design, architecture, api-contract, event-contract, data-schema, threat-model, spike, migration-plan, release-notes, deploy-plan, runbook, postmortem, tech-debt, diataxis-doc.
  • Regulated profile: brd, srs, use-case, traceability. If a project needs regulated documentation, its obligations decide what to add.
  • Spec sections for later: defect, ui-spec, decision-table, state-model, sequence, ui-checklist.
  • Standards: RGB, BCP14, CONVCOMMENTS, AGENTSMD, SCRUM, LEANCANVAS, JTBD, UC, ISO29148, ARC42, BLAMELESS, DIATAXIS, DESIGNMD, UML, C4, BPMN, DMN, OPENAPI, ASYNCAPI, JSONSCHEMA, DTCG, CSF, 3C, INVEST, EXMAP, ISO25010, WCAG, APG, STRIDE, ASVS, AAA, BVA.

Decisions

#QuestionDecisionReason
1Is a 3-level focus enough?Superseded by decision 15.—
2Is the minimum set too heavy?Split into a project set (once) and one spec per change.No "one size fits all".
3Relevance per change size?Superseded by decision 16. The change type guides the acceptance criteria.—
4META fields?id, type, title, status, created, updated, links. A spec adds change and impact (decision 43). See decision 20.Minimum that supports IDs, status, and traceability. The change type can change without a new ID.
5ADR format?MADR only.Current standard; its minimal variant covers the Nygard form.
6Standards for the remaining documents?None. Plain Markdown + META.YAGNI.
7Is progress-log a document?No. Progress lives in the tasks of the spec (decision 53).One source of truth for progress.
8Where do user stories live?Superseded by decision 27.—
9Spec-first or spec-anchored?Spec-first. Knowledge is harvested into LIVE documents.Specs stay small; living docs stay true.
10Where do CHG documents go after done?They stay in the same folder. Status done marks them.Links never break.
11How are document IDs assigned?Specs use one neutral sequence, s0001, with the file s0001-<short-slug>.spec.md. Plans and reviews reuse the spec name with .plan.md and .review.md. The change type goes in the change field, not in the ID. ADR IDs wait for the first ADR. The H1 spec uses this provisional rule; the spec template in H2 confirms or changes it. See document IDs.The first spec needs a clear rule. A type letter in the ID would force a rename when the type changes. The suffix groups the documents of one change.
12Review and verification: one document or two?Superseded by decision 32.—
13UI specification: document or section?A section of the spec, for later.Spec-first: UI behavior is part of the change. design-system keeps the durable part.
14Are prose LIVE documents wiki pages?Yes. The AIDDbot wiki starts in H1 (decision 19).One fact, one home.
15Which tags does a document need?Two: life and relevance.Phase, focus, and context did not change any decision for the next change.
16How many documents does a change need?One spec. A separate impl-plan or review-report only with an explicit criterion that a skill can check.Small changes stay light. The criterion is checkable.
17Which change types?chore, refactor, fix, feat. An epic only groups specs. No prd and no regulated profile for now.They wait for a real need.
18How large is the catalog?The documents that the lifecycle skills produce have tables. The others are names.The catalog follows the skill map, not one change at a time.
19Do the foundational documents move to docs/wiki/?Yes, in H1. AGENTS.md, README.md, CHANGELOG.md, PLAN.md, and DESIGN.md stay at the root.The wiki is the base of AIDDbot documentation. AIDDbot tests its own wiki before its skills help teams keep one.
20Which dates does META hold?created and updated, as ISO 8601 dates without time. They replace date.Readers and the wiki review see when the content changed. Git keeps the status history. Time adds noise and merge conflicts.
21Do all documents need META?No. agents, readme, and changelog have none.Tools read them at fixed names. Frontmatter shows as noise on GitHub.
22Which type has the project plan?roadmap, with one per project.It is a living document of milestones. The name does not clash with the plan step or the impl-plan.
23Which ID has the design system?design-system, with one per project.Single documents use their type as ID, like wiki pages use their topic.
24How are the change steps named?Superseded by decision 50.—
25Is Close a phase?No. It is the last step of a change. It returns knowledge to the Foundation documents.It does not check anything. It keeps knowledge.
26Where does clarification go?Inside Analysis, before a person approves the spec.Fewer steps and handoffs.
27Which sections has a spec?Three ## sections: Problem (goal, out of scope, 1 to 3 user stories), Solution (an accessible technical design and its tasks), and Verification (a checklist of up to 9 EARS requirements, each with its user story).The sections follow the problem, solution, verification views. User stories give the reason for each requirement.
28Is there a limit on the size of a spec?Yes. At most 3 user stories and 9 requirements. A larger change is split.Small changes are easier to review and verify. A script can check the limits.
29Which standard do the requirements use?EARS only. GWT waits for a real need.One syntax. EARS covers typical, state, optional, and error cases.
30When does a person approve the spec?Once, at the end of Design, before Implementation.The person sees the problem, the requirements, and the solution together. Small changes do Analysis and Design in one session.
31What changes in a spec after approval?Only its checkboxes and its status and updated fields.The spec stays short and stable. A script can check it. Evidence lives in the check outputs, and later in end-to-end tests.
32Where do failures and findings go?To a review-report, only when a requirement fails or the change has findings.Most changes need no report. The spec does not grow after approval.
33How are user stories and requirements coded?US<n> for a user story. US<n>R<m> for a requirement, numbered inside its user story. From another document: <spec id>-US<n>R<m>. Codes are inline code, with a hyphen before their text.Codes compose like document IDs (s0001-plan). A hyphen is easy to type. Inline code shows each character, as DESIGN.md asks for IDs.
34Can an accepted spec change before its implementation starts?Yes. It goes back to draft, a person rewrites it, and approves it again. After the implementation starts, decision 31 applies.s0002 needed a new scope after approval and before any code. A rewrite is cheaper than a new spec for the same change.
35How are the change flow and the status use written?As tables with fixed anchors and columns. Document IDs go in backticks.The knowledge explorer reads them. A table is easier to read and to check than a list.
36Do user stories follow a standard?Yes: USERSTORY, the As a, I want, so that form.The spec already used the form. A named standard lets a script and a review check it.
37How do Gherkin scenarios and EARS requirements work together?The spec keeps EARS requirements. Design writes Gherkin scenarios in a LIVE feature-file, tagged with the full requirement code. A person approves them with the spec. End-to-end tests run them. Decision 29 still applies to the requirements.EARS states the behavior in one line. Gherkin gives the steps that a test runs. The tag links each test to its requirement. The scenarios live on after the spec is frozen.
38Where do format, lint, and unit tests run?In Implementation, as deterministic quality checks. They pass before Verification. agents holds their commands.They check the code, not the behavior. Scripts and tools run them, not a judgment.
39What does Verification do?Two things: end-to-end tests run the scenarios, and an agent reviews the diff against the review gates. The review decides pass or changes needed. The gates are a section of agents.Tests check the behavior. The review checks what tests cannot see. Each project sets its own gates without a new document.
40Which design documents cover data and the domain?A Data model subsection in the spec Solution, with a Mermaid erDiagram, when the change touches data. Close harvests it into one LIVE domain-model with the DDD terms. er-model is not a separate document.One home for the domain and its data. The spec shows only what the change touches.
41How does Implementation show its internal steps?A quality checks table: build, format, lint, and unit tests, in this order. Foundation sets up their commands in agents.The code compiles, has one style, is clean, and has tests before any review. The project chooses the tools for its stack.
42Are the review gates fixed?No. AIDDbot ships three default gates: security, user experience, and maintainability. A project changes, removes, or adds gates in agents.Teams have different risks. The defaults give a good start with no configuration.
43Do all changes follow the same flow?No. Each change has an impact level: small, medium, or large. A small change has a short spec, no feature-file, and its approval in the pull request. A large change adds a review-report (decision 53 removed the impl-plan). The levels replace the criterion for separate documents. Decision 30 applies to medium and large changes.Minor changes move fast. Large changes get the coordination they need. The change type says what a change does, not how much process it needs.
44Who decides the impact level?A skill proposes it from criteria that it can check. A person confirms it. The spec holds it in the impact field.The criteria make the level consistent. The person sees risks that the criteria miss.
45Which artifacts does Implementation produce?code, unit-test, and check-report, as document types of the catalog. They have no META. The agent reads each check-report and fixes the code until the checks pass.People see the output of Implementation like the output of the other steps. The report closes the loop of self-correction and gives evidence to Verification.
46Where do the feature files live?One feature-file for each user story, as US<n>.feature in the spec folder. Each change has one folder, docs/specs/s<NNNN>-<short-slug>/, with spec.md, the feature files, plan.md, and review.md. The feature-file is CHG: it changes decision 37. The e2e-test is the LIVE part. Decision 11 keeps the IDs; only the paths change.The scenarios travel with their spec and their user stories. They give the details of each check and make the e2e tests easy to generate and to trace. One folder keeps the documents of a change together.
47Who writes the end-to-end tests, and where?Another agent instance, in Implementation, in its own package. It does not read or change the source code. Verification runs them and writes a test-report. The e2e package does not make a change large.An agent that writes both the code and its tests can make them agree without solving the problem. Tests from outside keep the check honest. The e2e package often uses another stack.
48How are the files of a change named?Each file name starts with the spec ID: s0002.spec.md, s0002.plan.md, s0002.review.md, and s0002-US1.feature. The folder keeps its slug. It changes the file names of decision 46.With several files open in an editor, the tab shows which change and which document it is. The feature file name matches its Feature tag.
49How does the catalog mark code and tests?A third tag, Form: DOC for text that people and agents read, and CODE for source code and tests that tools run. The document catalog has a Form column after Life. The rows follow the lifecycle: project documents, then change documents in step order, and the changelog last.The knowledge explorer finds the project brain (LIVE and DOC) with no hard-coded IDs. The row order is the order of the brain on the map.
50How do the change steps relate to the lifecycle phases?The change flow is the work of the Development phase. Its steps are Analysis, Design, Implementation, Verification, and Close. A step name is not a phase name. Close writes the changelog entry to Unreleased, and Release reads it. It replaces decision 24.Each name is used once, at one level. Many changes close before one release. Intent decisions 1 and 9
51What is the ID of the agent instructions?agents.The ID follows the file name AGENTS.md, as readme and changelog do.
52Does the roadmap become a prd?No. The roadmap holds past and future milestones. prd stays a name for later.A PRD says what the product must do and why. A roadmap says when.
53Does the catalog keep an impl-plan?No. It is a name for later. A large change tracks its progress in the Tasks of the spec. It changes decision 43.Frontier models write good code without a separate plan file. One checklist is one source of truth (decision 7).
54In which step is the feature-file written?Analysis, with declarative scenarios and no interface steps. A person still approves the spec and its scenarios once, at the end of Design (decision 30).The scenarios are examples of the requirements. They describe the problem, not the solution.
55What does Analysis use and change?It reads the roadmap, glossary, wiki-page, domain-model, adr, and agents of the project brain. It writes the spec and the feature-file, and updates the roadmap when the work splits into several changes. Close harvests the rest.Analysis needs the whole brain to frame the problem. Spec-first: other knowledge waits for Close.
56Does the impact levels table name the documents of each level?Yes. The columns Skips and Adds hold document IDs. small skips feature-file, e2e-test, and test-report. large adds review-report. The knowledge explorer reads the table. s0005The explorer filters the change loop map by impact level. The wiki contract allows no document ID in the code.

docs.title: AIDDbot Explorer Development
docs.html:
AIDDbot Explorer Development

How we build the knowledge explorer: a static web site that tells the story of AIDDbot to people. It reads the AIDDbot documents and never edits them. It does not ship. s0002

Status: draft.

Commands

Run them from the repository root. The explorer is the only package, so there is no Bun workspace yet. Scaffolding

TaskCommand
Install the explorer dependencies (once)bun run explorer:install
Build the site in packages/explorer/dist/bun run explorer:build
Build and publish the site to GitHub Pagesbun run explorer:publish
Serve the site at http://localhost:4173/ and build it again on each change. A change to the builder code restarts the server.bun run explorer:dev
Type-checkbunx tsc --noEmit in packages/explorer/
Testbun test in packages/explorer/
Lintbun lint (see the open point)

The build accepts --root <repository> and --out <folder>. The site works from any folder of a static file server, because all its paths are relative and the views use hash addresses.

Publication

Use bun run explorer:publish when you want to update the public explorer. The script needs Git access to push to origin. It fetches origin/main, installs the locked dependencies, and builds that commit in a temporary checkout on your machine.

The script pushes the generated site to gh-pages. Its commit message records the source commit. In Settings → Pages, GitHub Pages uses Deploy from a branch, with gh-pages and /(root) selected. The .nojekyll file tells Pages to serve the generated files as they are. GitHub Pages publishing source

Folders

packages/explorer/
├── package.json            # Pinned dependencies and the build, dev, and test scripts
├── tsconfig.json
├── src/
│   ├── build.ts            # Entry point of the build
│   ├── dev.ts              # Development server
│   ├── publish.ts          # Builds a source commit and pushes the site to gh-pages
│   ├── shared/types.ts     # The data file format, shared by the builder and the site
│   ├── builder/            # Runs on Bun: reads the documents and writes the site
│   └── site/               # Runs in the browser: HTML, CSS, and custom elements
├── test/                   # bun:test tests
└── dist/                   # Build output. Git ignores it.

Wiki contract

The builder reads seven tables. Each one is the first table under a fixed heading. The column names are fixed.

TableHeading anchorColumns
Lifecycle phasesintent.md#lifecycle-phases#, Phase, Work, Uses, Produces
Change flowdocumentation-catalog.md#change-flow#, Step, Work, Uses, Produces
Impact levelsdocumentation-catalog.md#impact-levelsImpact, When, Flow, Skips, Adds
Building blocksintent.md#building-blocksBlock, Role, Relations
Document catalogdocumentation-catalog.md#document-catalogID, Document, Life, Form, Relevance, Standards, Purpose
Form tagdocumentation-catalog.md#formCode, Form, Rule
Status usedocumentation-catalog.md#status-useStatus, Meaning, Set in, Used by

Rules:

  • ID columns. Uses, Produces, Used by, Skips, and Adds hold document IDs in backticks. Plain text is allowed next to them, such as "code, and docs".
  • Name columns. Relations and Set in hold a comma list. Each item is a document ID in backticks, or the name of a phase, a step, or a block. Phase and step names are unique.
  • Links between elements. Every step links to the phase whose row links to the change flow: Development. No phase name is written in the code. Every reference links both elements.
  • Form. Each catalog row holds one code of the Form tag table in backticks. A missing Form column or an unknown value stops the build.
  • Project brain. The brain holds every document type with Life LIVE and Form DOC, in catalog order. No document ID is written in the code.
  • Impact levels. Skips names the document types that the change loop map hides for the level. Adds names the document types that it marks as required. The level name is the code in backticks of the Impact cell.
  • Sections. A relative link in a row cell adds the linked section to the page of the element. A link to a glossary anchor adds a glossary term. The page also shows the glossary term with the ID or the name of the element, and, for a document type, the catalog section with its ID, such as #spec.
  • Errors. A missing heading or table, a renamed or missing column, an unknown document ID, an unknown Form value, or an unknown name stops the build. The error names the file and the problem.
  • Smaller problems. A missing or invalid META, a broken relative link, or an unknown links value does not stop the build. The build lists each one with its file. The document shows a warning.

A change to these headings or columns needs a change to the builder in the same commit. Page rules

Content scope

GroupFiles
Wikidocs/wiki/*.md
RootREADME.md, AGENTS.md, PLAN.md, DESIGN.md, CHANGELOG.md
Specsdocs/specs/**/*.md
  • README.md, AGENTS.md, and CHANGELOG.md have no META by design. Their type comes from the file name: readme, agents, and changelog.
  • DESIGN.md keeps its META under the aiddbot key.
  • A link to another file of the repository, such as LICENSE or a folder, shows as plain text with an "outside the explorer" mark.

Map rules

Code places every element. Nobody draws a map by hand. The information comes in layers: an overview, two detail maps, and the element pages.

AddressMapShows
#/OverviewThe phases, the project brain as one box, and the steps as boxes
#/map/changeChange loopThe steps, their document types, and the brain band
#/map/brainProject brainThe brain document types between the phases and the steps
#/blocksBuilding blocksA list of the building blocks. It is a view, not a map.
 
OVERVIEW   Foundation ──► Development ──► Release ──► Maintenance
                              │ zoom          ▲            │
                              ▼               │  feedback  │
           ┌─ PROJECT BRAIN ──────────────────┴──┐ ◄───────┘
           └─────────────────────────────────────┘
           Analysis ► Design ► Implementation ► Verification ► Close

CHANGE     │ readme  glossary  wiki-page  agents  roadmap  adr  ... │
LOOP       Analysis ► Design ► Implementation ► Verification ► Close
           spec       ...       code             test-report
           [ small | medium | large ]

BRAIN      Foundation  Development  Release  Maintenance
           │ readme  glossary  wiki-page  agents  roadmap  adr  ... │
           Analysis    Design   Implementation   Verification   Close
  • Overview. The phases form the top row, in table order. A dashed arrow, the feedback loop, goes from the last phase to the phase that holds the change flow. The brain is one prominent box with its name only. The steps form the bottom row, in table order, inside a frame. A zoom line goes from the phase that holds the change flow to the frame. A link joins a phase or a step to the brain box when its Uses or Produces holds a brain document type. An element that reads and writes the brain gets one line with two heads. The overview shows no document type and no building block.
  • Clicks on the overview. A phase opens its page. The brain box opens the brain map. The change loop frame or a step opens the change loop map.
  • Change loop map. The brain document types form the top row, in catalog order, under the heading Project brain. The steps form a row below it, under the heading Change loop. The map has no frames. A brain document type ID with a hyphen shows in two lines. Any other document type hangs under the first step that produces it, or else under the first step that uses it. The map always draws the links from the last step to the brain. The links of the other steps show when a person points at the step.
  • Impact filter. The change loop map has a selector with the levels of the impact levels table. The default is medium. A level hides the document types in its Skips cell and marks the document types in its Adds cell as required.
  • Brain map. The phases form the top row, the brain document types the middle row, and the steps the bottom row. Each row has a heading: Project loop, Project brain, and Change loop. The map has no frames. An ID with a hyphen shows in two lines, such as wiki-page. A person who points at an element sees only its active links: who writes and who reads each brain document type. The arrow heads of these links are larger than the heads of the main arrows.
  • Read and write links. An element that reads and writes the same brain document type gets one line with two heads, on every map.
  • Blocks view. It lists every building block in table order, with its role and a link to its page. The header links to it.
  • Parent map. Each element has one parent map. A phase has the overview. A step has the change loop map. A brain document type has the brain map. Any other document type has the change loop map. A block has the blocks view. The builder sets it from these rules, with no element ID in the code.
  • Breadcrumbs. An element page shows the path from the overview through the parent map to the element, such as Map › Change loop › Design. Each part is a link.
  • Mini-map. An element page draws its parent map in small, with the element marked. A click opens that map.
  • Phase page. The phase diagram shows Uses and Produces, as the step diagram does. The page of the phase that holds the change flow also shows its steps.

Site rules

  • Components. Each part of the screen is one custom element in its own file in src/site/components/. There is no UI framework and no shadow DOM, so the global styles apply.
  • Views. #/ is the overview. #/map/change and #/map/brain are the detail maps. #/blocks is the blocks view. #/<kind>/<id> is an element page, with the kinds phase, step, block, and type. #/doc/<id> and #/doc/<id>/<anchor> are full documents. Any other address shows the not-found view.
  • Theme. The builder turns the colors and fonts of DESIGN.md into theme.css. Dark is the default. The theme button saves the choice in the browser.
  • Fonts. The @fontsource packages give the Latin subsets of Audiowide, Roboto, and Fira Code. The bundler puts them in styles.css.
  • Motion. Diagrams and the map zoom use the Web Animations API. With reduced motion, every diagram shows its final state and a click opens the page with no zoom.
  • Mermaid. The site loads mermaid only when a full document has a Mermaid block.

Open points

  • bun lint does not exist in Bun 1.4.5. The command fails with Script not found "lint". AGENTS.md and CLI development ask for it.
  • Bun.markdown heading ids are not GitHub slugs. The builder adds its own.
  • The logo and the favicon load from the author's site. Offline, the header and the browser tab show no icon.
